chapter_title:
CHAPTER VI

A CAMP OF THE RESERVE
text:
Not many people visited this house. Every Wednesday evening, from
half-past eight to eleven, Miss Barfoot was at home to any of her
acquaintances, including her pupils, who chose to call upon her; but
this was in the nature of an association with recognized objects. Of
society in the common sense Miss Barfoot saw very little; she had no
time to sacrifice in the pursuit of idle ceremonies. By the successive
deaths of two relatives, a widowed sister and an uncle, she had come
into possession of a modest fortune; but no thought of a life such as
would have suggested itself to most women in her place ever tempted
her. Her studies had always been of a very positive nature; her
abilities were of a kind uncommon in women, or at all events very
rarely developed in one of her sex. She could have managed a large and
complicated business, could have filled a place on a board of
directors, have taken an active part in municipal government—nay,
perchance in national. And this turn of intellect consisted with many
traits of character so strongly feminine that people who knew her best
thought of her with as much tenderness as admiration. She did not seek
to become known as the leader of a “movement,” yet her quiet work was
probably more effectual than the public career of women who
propagandize for female emancipation. Her aim was to draw from the
overstocked profession of teaching as many capable young women as she
could lay hands on, and to fit them for certain of the pursuits
nowadays thrown open to their sex. She held the conviction that
whatever man could do, woman could do equally well—those tasks only
excepted which demand great physical strength. At her instance, and
with help from her purse, two girls were preparing themselves to be
pharmaceutical chemists; two others had been aided by her to open a
bookseller’s shop; and several who had clerkships in view received an
admirable training at her school in Great Portland Street.

enrichment.interest_rationale: Rich, comprehensive exposition of Barfoot's background, values, and educational enterprise: she is an uncommon woman of business acumen and refined character, with progressive ideas about female education and capabilities, yet surprisingly modest impact-seeking.
enrichment.best_quote: She did not seek to become known as the leader of a 'movement,' yet her quiet work was probably more effectual than the public career of women who propagandize for female emancipation.
enrichment.summary: The narrator provides extensive background on Miss Barfoot's financial independence, intellectual abilities, and educational mission: she draws capable young women from teaching to train for new professions through her Great Portland Street school, believing women equal to men except in tasks requiring great strength.

chapter_title:
CHAPTER VI

A CAMP OF THE RESERVE
text:
Thither every weekday morning Miss Barfoot and Rhoda repaired; they
arrived at nine o’clock, and with an hour’s interval work went on until
five.

enrichment.interest_rationale: Routine description of the school's daily schedule; minimal interest or significance.
enrichment.summary: Miss Barfoot and Rhoda work at the Great Portland Street school from nine o'clock to five daily with a one-hour break.

chapter_title:
CHAPTER VI

A CAMP OF THE RESERVE
text:
Entering by the private door of a picture-cleaner’s shop, they ascended
to the second story, where two rooms had been furnished like
comfortable offices; two smaller on the floor above served for
dressing-rooms. In one of the offices, typewriting and occasionally
other kinds of work that demanded intelligence were carried on by three
or four young women regularly employed. To superintend this department
was Miss Nunn’s chief duty, together with business correspondence under
the principal’s direction. In the second room Miss Barfoot instructed
her pupils, never more than three being with her at a time. A bookcase
full of works on the Woman Question and allied topics served as a
circulating library; volumes were lent without charge to the members of
this little society. Once a month Miss Barfoot or Miss Nunn, by turns,
gave a brief address on some set subject; the hour was four o’clock,
and about a dozen hearers generally assembled. Both worked very hard.
Miss Barfoot did not look upon her enterprise as a source of pecuniary
profit, but she had made the establishment more than self-supporting.
Her pupils increased in number, and the working department promised
occupation for a larger staff than was at present engaged. The young
women in general answered their friend’s expectations, but of course
there were disappointing instances. One of these had caused Miss
Barfoot special distress. A young girl whom she had released from a
life of much hardship, and who, after a couple of months’ trial, bade
fair to develop noteworthy ability, of a sudden disappeared. She was
without relatives in London, and Miss Barfoot’s endeavours to find her
proved for several weeks very futile. Then came news of her; she was
living as the mistress of a married man. Every effort was made to bring
her back, but the girl resisted; presently she again passed out of
sight, and now more than a year had elapsed since Miss Barfoot’s last
interview with her.

enrichment.interest_rationale: Detailed, vivid account of the school's physical setup and operations; introduction of Bella Royston's tragedy as the climax—a gifted pupil who was seduced by a married man and disappeared into mistressdom, representing both the hope and peril of female independence. Exceptionally significant for the chapter's central conflict.
enrichment.best_quote: A young girl whom she had released from a life of much hardship, and who, after a couple of months' trial, bade fair to develop noteworthy ability, of a sudden disappeared. She was without relatives in London, and Miss Barfoot's endeavours to find her proved for several weeks very futile. Then came news of her; she was living as the mistress of a married man.
enrichment.summary: The narrator describes the school's setup and operations in detail, culminating in the tragic account of Bella Royston: a talented pupil whom Barfoot had removed from hardship, who showed promise, but who abandoned the school to become the mistress of a married man, resisting all efforts to rescue her.

chapter_title:
CHAPTER VI

A CAMP OF THE RESERVE
text:
This Monday morning, among letters delivered at the house, was one from
the strayed girl. Miss Barfoot read it in private, and throughout the
day remained unusually grave. At five o’clock, when staff and pupils
had all departed, she sat for a while in meditation, then spoke to
Rhoda, who was glancing over a book by the window.

enrichment.interest_rationale: The catalyst moment: a letter arrives from Bella Royston after more than a year, troubling Barfoot greatly and setting up the entire chapter's moral and philosophical conflict.
enrichment.summary: A Monday morning letter arrives from Bella Royston; Barfoot reads it privately and remains troubled throughout the day, finally sharing it with Rhoda at five o'clock.

chapter_title:
CHAPTER VI

A CAMP OF THE RESERVE
text: “Here’s a letter I should like you to read.”

enrichment.interest_rationale: Barfoot's simple request for Rhoda to read the letter; minimal substance.
enrichment.summary: Miss Barfoot asks Rhoda to read the letter.

chapter_title:
CHAPTER VI

A CAMP OF THE RESERVE
text: “Something that has been troubling you since morning, isn’t it?”

enrichment.interest_rationale: Rhoda's perceptive observation that something has troubled Barfoot since morning; shows Rhoda's attention to her friend but adds little substance.
enrichment.summary: Rhoda observes that Barfoot has been troubled since morning.

chapter_title:
CHAPTER VI

A CAMP OF THE RESERVE
text: “Yes.”

enrichment.interest_rationale: Barfoot's brief confirmation; no content.
enrichment.summary: Miss Barfoot confirms Rhoda's observation.

chapter_title:
CHAPTER VI

A CAMP OF THE RESERVE
text:
Rhoda took the sheet and quickly ran through its contents. Her face
hardened, and she threw down the letter with a smile of contempt.

enrichment.interest_rationale: Rhoda's immediate negative reaction: she reads quickly, her face hardens, and she responds with contempt, setting the stage for their conflict.
enrichment.summary: Rhoda reads the letter quickly, her face hardens, and she throws it down with a contemptuous smile.

chapter_title:
CHAPTER VI

A CAMP OF THE RESERVE
text: “What do you advise?” asked the elder woman, closely observing her.

enrichment.interest_rationale: Barfoot's careful inquiry after Rhoda's reaction; begins the dialogue but without force.
enrichment.summary: Miss Barfoot asks Rhoda what she advises, watching her closely.

chapter_title:
CHAPTER VI

A CAMP OF THE RESERVE
text: “An answer in two lines—with a cheque enclosed, if you see fit.”

enrichment.interest_rationale: Rhoda's stark response: a two-line answer and a cheque, dismissing Bella's plea; reveals Rhoda's hardness and utilitarian view of charity.
enrichment.best_quote: An answer in two lines—with a cheque enclosed, if you see fit.
enrichment.summary: Rhoda advises a curt reply and perhaps a cheque, treating the matter as closed.

chapter_title:
CHAPTER VI

A CAMP OF THE RESERVE
text: “Does that really meet the case?”

enrichment.interest_rationale: Barfoot's questioning whether Rhoda's approach addresses the real situation; opens the debate without clarity.
enrichment.summary: Miss Barfoot questions whether a curt reply truly addresses Bella's situation.

chapter_title:
CHAPTER VI

A CAMP OF THE RESERVE
text: “More than meets it, I should say.”

enrichment.interest_rationale: Rhoda's brief assertion; no substantive content.
enrichment.summary: Rhoda insists her approach more than addresses the situation.

chapter_title:
CHAPTER VI

A CAMP OF THE RESERVE
text: Miss Barfoot pondered.

enrichment.interest_rationale: Barfoot's brief reflection; transition to the substantive debate.
enrichment.summary: Miss Barfoot pauses in thought.

chapter_title:
CHAPTER VI

A CAMP OF THE RESERVE
text:
“I am doubtful. That is a letter of despair, and I can’t close my ears
to it.”

enrichment.interest_rationale: Barfoot's key assertion: the letter expresses despair and she cannot ignore it; introduces her compassionate position against Rhoda's severity.
enrichment.best_quote: That is a letter of despair, and I can't close my ears to it.
enrichment.summary: Barfoot declares that Bella's letter is one of despair and she cannot ignore it.

chapter_title:
CHAPTER VI

A CAMP OF THE RESERVE
text:
“You had an affection for the girl. Help her, by all means, if you feel
compelled to. But you would hardly dream of taking her back again?”

enrichment.interest_rationale: Rhoda's grudging admission of Barfoot's affection while suggesting practical help is distinct from re-admittance; foreshadows the crux of their disagreement.
enrichment.summary: Rhoda acknowledges Barfoot's affection for Bella and permits her to help, but questions whether she would take her back as a pupil.

chapter_title:
CHAPTER VI

A CAMP OF THE RESERVE
text: “That’s the point. Why shouldn’t I?”

enrichment.interest_rationale: Barfoot's simple question that becomes the centre of the entire debate: 'Why shouldn't I?'—asserting her autonomy against Rhoda's prescriptive judgement.
enrichment.best_quote: Why shouldn't I?
enrichment.summary: Barfoot poses the central question: why should she not take Bella back as a pupil?

chapter_title:
CHAPTER VI

A CAMP OF THE RESERVE
text:
“For one thing,” replied Rhoda, looking coldly down upon her friend,
“you will never do any good with her. For another, she isn’t a suitable
companion for the girls she would meet here.”

enrichment.interest_rationale: Rhoda's two objections: Bella cannot be reformed and she is unsuitable company; establishes Rhoda's utilitarian and classifying view of women.
enrichment.summary: Rhoda offers two objections: Bella cannot be helped, and she is unsuitable company for the other pupils.

chapter_title:
CHAPTER VI

A CAMP OF THE RESERVE
text:
“I can’t be sure of either objection. She acted with deplorable
rashness, with infatuation, but I never discovered any sign of evil in
her. Did you?”

enrichment.interest_rationale: Barfoot challenges Rhoda's assumptions: Bella showed no sign of fundamental evil; the action, though rash, was not inherently corrupt; this initiates her compassionate counter-argument.
enrichment.summary: Barfoot disputes Rhoda's claim that Bella showed signs of evil; she argues that rash infatuation is not inherent depravity.

chapter_title:
CHAPTER VI

A CAMP OF THE RESERVE
text:
“Evil? Well, what does the word mean? I am not a Puritan, and I don’t
judge her as the ordinary woman would. But I think she has put herself
altogether beyond our sympathy. She was twenty-two years old—no
child—and she acted with her eyes open. No deceit was practised with
her. She knew the man had a wife, and she was base enough to accept a
share of his attentions. Do you advocate polygamy? That is an
intelligible position, I admit. It is one way of meeting the social
difficulty. But not mine.”

enrichment.interest_rationale: Rhoda's extended argument: she defines Bella's act as base collusion in adultery with full knowledge; rejects 'polygamy' and insists that women must demonstrate sexual self-restraint. Reveals Rhoda's ascetic feminist philosophy and intransigence.
enrichment.best_quote: She was base enough to accept a share of his attentions. Do you advocate polygamy? That is an intelligible position, I admit. It is one way of meeting the social difficulty. But not mine.
enrichment.summary: Rhoda condemns Bella for knowingly becoming an adulteress with open eyes, rejecting the notion that this can be forgiven, and frames it as an issue of sexual self-restraint essential to female emancipation.

chapter_title:
CHAPTER VI

A CAMP OF THE RESERVE
text: “My dear Rhoda, don’t enrage yourself.”

enrichment.interest_rationale: Barfoot's soft entreaty that Rhoda calm herself; tone management rather than substantive argument.
enrichment.summary: Barfoot gently asks Rhoda not to be angry.

chapter_title:
CHAPTER VI

A CAMP OF THE RESERVE
text: “I will try not to.”

enrichment.interest_rationale: Rhoda's brief concession to try to control herself; minimal content.
enrichment.summary: Rhoda promises to try not to become angry.

chapter_title:
CHAPTER VI

A CAMP OF THE RESERVE
text:
“But I can’t see the temptation to do so. Come and sit down, and talk
quietly. No, I have no fondness for polygamy. I find it very hard to
understand how she could act as she did. But a mistake, however
wretched, mustn’t condemn a woman for life. That’s the way of the
world, and decidedly it mustn’t be ours.”

enrichment.interest_rationale: Barfoot's substantive counter: while sympathizing with Bella's weakness, she argues that a single mistake must not condemn a woman for life and that this philosophy must distinguish them from the world's harshness. Core statement of her position.
enrichment.best_quote: A mistake, however wretched, mustn't condemn a woman for life. That's the way of the world, and decidedly it mustn't be ours.
enrichment.summary: Barfoot argues that a single error must not be lifelong punishment; that such compassion should distinguish their endeavor from worldly harshness.

chapter_title:
CHAPTER VI

A CAMP OF THE RESERVE
text: “On this point I practically agree with the world.”

enrichment.interest_rationale: Rhoda's blunt admission of alignment with conventional morality; shows her divergence from Barfoot but stated plainly.
enrichment.summary: Rhoda admits she practically agrees with conventional morality on this point.

chapter_title:
CHAPTER VI

A CAMP OF THE RESERVE
text:
“I see you do, and it astonishes me. You are going through curious
changes, in several respects. A year ago you didn’t speak of her like
this.”

enrichment.interest_rationale: Barfoot observes that Rhoda has changed her views over the year they have known each other; notes Rhoda's increasing severity and ideological hardening.
enrichment.best_quote: You are going through curious changes, in several respects. A year ago you didn't speak of her like this.
enrichment.summary: Barfoot notes that Rhoda has become more severe and has changed her views on Bella's case from a year earlier.

chapter_title:
CHAPTER VI

A CAMP OF THE RESERVE
text:
“Partly because I didn’t know you well enough to speak my mind. Partly
yes, I have changed a good deal, no doubt. But I should never have
proposed to take her by the hand and let bygones be bygones. That is an
amiable impulse, but anti-social.”

enrichment.interest_rationale: Rhoda's explanation: she was formerly restrained by lack of intimacy; now she admits transformation but denies she would have been merciful a year ago either. Shows her consistency in rigour.
enrichment.summary: Rhoda explains that earlier restraint was due to less intimacy with Barfoot, and clarifies that her core position has always been one of severity regarding Bella's case.

chapter_title:
CHAPTER VI

A CAMP OF THE RESERVE
text: “A favourite word on your lips just now, Rhoda. Why is it anti-social?”

enrichment.interest_rationale: Barfoot's challenge to Rhoda's use of 'anti-social'; requests explanation without developing substantively.
enrichment.summary: Barfoot questions Rhoda's frequent use of 'anti-social' and asks her to explain why mercy toward Bella would be anti-social.

chapter_title:
CHAPTER VI

A CAMP OF THE RESERVE
text:
“Because one of the supreme social needs of our day is the education of
women in self-respect and self-restraint. There are plenty of
people—men chiefly, but a few women also of a certain temperament—who
cry for a reckless individualism in these matters. They would tell you
that she behaved laudably, that she was  living out herself —and
things of that kind. But I didn’t think you shared such views.”

enrichment.interest_rationale: Rhoda's passionate core argument: women must be educated in self-respect and restraint; permitting Bella's return teaches laxity that undermines female advancement; refutes individualistic positions. Central articulation of her ascetic feminist vision.
enrichment.best_quote: Because one of the supreme social needs of our day is the education of women in self-respect and self-restraint.
enrichment.summary: Rhoda explains that the core social need is female education in self-respect and restraint; others advocate reckless individualism, but she finds that dangerous to women's emancipation.

chapter_title:
CHAPTER VI

A CAMP OF THE RESERVE
text:
“I don’t, altogether. “The education of women in self-respect.” Very
well. Here is a poor woman whose self-respect has given way under
grievous temptation. Circumstances have taught her that she made a wild
mistake. The man gives her up, and bids her live as she can; she is
reduced to beggary. Now, in that position a girl is tempted to sink
still further. The letter of two lines and an enclosed cheque would as
likely as not plunge her into depths from which she could never be
rescued. It would assure her that there was no hope. On the other hand,
we have it in our power to attempt that very education of which you
speak. She has brains, and doesn’t belong to the vulgar. It seems to me
that you are moved by illogical impulses—and certainly anything but
kind ones.”

enrichment.interest_rationale: Barfoot's masterful counter-argument: she reinterprets Rhoda's logic compassionately—Bella's self-respect is shattered, and the two-line response would guarantee despair and further descent, whereas re-admission offers education and recovery. Challenges Rhoda's cruelty as illogical.
enrichment.best_quote: The letter of two lines and an enclosed cheque would as likely as not plunge her into depths from which she could never be rescued. It would assure her that there was no hope.
enrichment.summary: Barfoot argues that Rhoda's proposed coldness would drive Bella to greater ruin, while re-admission would offer the very education in self-respect Rhoda claims to champion.

chapter_title:
CHAPTER VI

A CAMP OF THE RESERVE
text: Rhoda only grew more stubborn.

enrichment.interest_rationale: Brief narrative that Rhoda becomes more stubborn; transition without substance.
enrichment.summary: Rhoda grows more stubborn in her position.

chapter_title:
CHAPTER VI

A CAMP OF THE RESERVE
text:
“You say she yielded to a grievous temptation. What temptation? Will it
bear putting into words?”

enrichment.interest_rationale: Rhoda's challenging question: what is the temptation that led Bella astray?—implying it cannot be named or justified, which will provoke Barfoot's counter.
enrichment.summary: Rhoda challenges Barfoot to state what temptation Bella yielded to, questioning whether it can be named without moral justification.

chapter_title:
CHAPTER VI

A CAMP OF THE RESERVE
text:
“Oh yes, I think it will,” answered Miss Barfoot, with her gentlest
smile. “She fell in love with the man.”

enrichment.interest_rationale: Barfoot's simple, brave answer: 'She fell in love with the man'—states what Rhoda will not name and suggests it is a real human experience worthy of consideration.
enrichment.best_quote: She fell in love with the man.
enrichment.summary: Barfoot simply states that Bella fell in love with the man.

chapter_title:
CHAPTER VI

A CAMP OF THE RESERVE
text:
“Fell in love!” Concentration of scorn was in this echo. “Oh, for what
isn’t that phrase responsible!”

enrichment.interest_rationale: Rhoda's scornful echo—'Fell in love!'—expresses contempt for romantic love as vaporous nonsense; reveals her deep suspicion of the emotion as central to women's subjugation.
enrichment.best_quote: Fell in love! Concentration of scorn was in this echo.
enrichment.summary: Rhoda echoes 'Fell in love!' with scorn, questioning what follies are justified by that phrase.

chapter_title:
CHAPTER VI

A CAMP OF THE RESERVE
text:
“Rhoda, let me ask you a question on which I have never ventured. Do
you know what it is to be in love?”

enrichment.interest_rationale: Barfoot's crucial personal question to Rhoda: 'Do you know what it is to be in love?'—opening an intimate interrogation that will reveal Rhoda's emotional history and limits.
enrichment.best_quote: Do you know what it is to be in love?
enrichment.summary: Barfoot asks Rhoda directly whether she has ever experienced love.

chapter_title:
CHAPTER VI

A CAMP OF THE RESERVE
text:
Miss Nunn’s strong features were moved as if by a suppressed laugh; the
colour of her cheeks grew very slightly warm.

enrichment.interest_rationale: Rhoda's visible response to the question: a suppressed laugh and slight warmth in her cheeks; suggests she feels the question's force but resists vulnerability.
enrichment.summary: Rhoda's strong features show suppressed emotion; her cheeks flush slightly, suggesting the question strikes at something real.

chapter_title:
CHAPTER VI

A CAMP OF THE RESERVE
text:
“I am a normal human being,” she answered, with an impatient gesture.
“I understand perfectly well what the phrase signifies.”

enrichment.interest_rationale: Rhoda's defensive reply; claims understanding while avoiding the personal question.
enrichment.summary: Rhoda asserts she understands the phrase perfectly well as a normal human being.

chapter_title:
CHAPTER VI

A CAMP OF THE RESERVE
text: “That is no answer, my dear. Have you ever been in love with any man?”

enrichment.interest_rationale: Barfoot's pressing follow-up: 'Have you ever been in love with any man?'—directly probing Rhoda's emotional history and challenging her authority to judge Bella.
enrichment.best_quote: Have you ever been in love with any man?
enrichment.summary: Barfoot presses Rhoda for a personal answer: has she ever been in love?

chapter_title:
CHAPTER VI

A CAMP OF THE RESERVE
text: “Yes. When I was fifteen.”

enrichment.interest_rationale: Rhoda's grudging admission: she was in love at fifteen; reveals a past self vulnerable to emotion, suggesting her current severity is a defensive hardening.
enrichment.best_quote: Yes. When I was fifteen.
enrichment.summary: Rhoda admits she was in love once, at age fifteen.

chapter_title:
CHAPTER VI

A CAMP OF THE RESERVE
text:
“And not since,” rejoined the other, shaking her head and smiling. “No,
not since?”

enrichment.interest_rationale: Barfoot's knowing follow-up: 'And not since?'—probing whether Rhoda has since steeled herself against love or whether she is simply without it.
enrichment.summary: Barfoot presses whether Rhoda has loved again since fifteen.

chapter_title:
CHAPTER VI

A CAMP OF THE RESERVE
text: “Thank Heaven, no!”

enrichment.interest_rationale: Rhoda's firm answer: 'Thank Heaven, no!'—expresses relief at emotional freedom, suggesting she has fought against romantic attachment.
enrichment.best_quote: Thank Heaven, no!
enrichment.summary: Rhoda declares with gratitude that she has not loved since, suggesting emotional freedom as a blessing.

chapter_title:
CHAPTER VI

A CAMP OF THE RESERVE
text:
“Then you are not very well able to judge this case. I, on the other
hand, can judge it with the very largest understanding. Don’t smile so
witheringly, Rhoda. I shall neglect your advice for once.”

enrichment.interest_rationale: Barfoot's conclusive statement: Rhoda's lack of experience in love disqualifies her from judging Bella's case; Barfoot, by contrast, can judge with 'largest understanding'; asserts Barfoot's emotional authority and resolves to override Rhoda's advice.
enrichment.best_quote: Then you are not very well able to judge this case. I, on the other hand, can judge it with the very largest understanding.
enrichment.summary: Barfoot concludes that Rhoda's emotional inexperience disqualifies her judgment, while Barfoot's own experience enables broader understanding; she decides to act independently.

chapter_title:
CHAPTER VI

A CAMP OF THE RESERVE
text: “You will bring this girl back, and continue teaching her as before?”

enrichment.interest_rationale: Rhoda's confirmatory question, beginning to articulate the practical consequences of Barfoot's decision.
enrichment.summary: Rhoda asks whether Barfoot will bring Bella back and continue instructing her.

chapter_title:
CHAPTER VI

A CAMP OF THE RESERVE
text:
“We have no one here that knows her, and with prudence she need never
be talked about by those of our friends who did.”

enrichment.interest_rationale: Barfoot's practical reassurance: Bella is unknown to present pupils; with prudence she can be kept quiet; suggests Barfoot is considering practical safeguards while remaining compassionate.
enrichment.summary: Barfoot notes that Bella is unknown to current pupils and can be managed discreetly.

chapter_title:
CHAPTER VI

A CAMP OF THE RESERVE
text: “Oh, weak—weak—weak!”

enrichment.interest_rationale: Rhoda's dismissive exclamation: 'Weak—weak—weak!'—judges Barfoot's position as morally and strategically deficient; short but emotionally forceful.
enrichment.best_quote: Weak—weak—weak!
enrichment.summary: Rhoda rejects Barfoot's plan as weak in principle and practice.

chapter_title:
CHAPTER VI

A CAMP OF THE RESERVE
text: “For once I must act independently.”

enrichment.interest_rationale: Barfoot's assertion of her autonomous decision; resolves the immediate conflict but without elaboration.
enrichment.summary: Barfoot declares she must act independently on this matter.

chapter_title:
CHAPTER VI

A CAMP OF THE RESERVE
text:
“Yes, and at a stroke change the whole character of your work. You
never proposed keeping a reformatory. Your aim is to help chosen girls,
who promise to be of some use in the world. This Miss Royston
represents the profitless average—no, she is below the average. Are
you so blind as to imagine that any good will ever come of such a
person? If you wish to save her from the streets, do so by all means.
But to put her among your chosen pupils is to threaten your whole
undertaking. Let it once become known—and it  would  become
known—that a girl of that character came here, and your usefulness is
at an end. In a year’s time you will have to choose between giving up
the school altogether and making it a refuge for outcasts.”

enrichment.interest_rationale: Rhoda's extended final argument: Bella represents the 'profitless average'; admitting her would destroy the school's purpose and reputation; would force choice between pure education or reformatory; reveals Rhoda's strategic, utilitarian vision but also ideological extremity and classism.
enrichment.best_quote: In a year's time you will have to choose between giving up the school altogether and making it a refuge for outcasts.
enrichment.summary: Rhoda argues that Bella is below the average and that taking her back would transform the school into a reformatory, destroying its effectiveness and reputation; threatens the entire enterprise.

chapter_title:
CHAPTER VI

A CAMP OF THE RESERVE
text: Miss Barfoot was silent. She tapped with her fingers on the table.

enrichment.interest_rationale: Barfoot's silent response: she taps the table, suggesting inner conflict but offering no verbal reply.
enrichment.summary: Miss Barfoot is silent; she taps her fingers on the table, remaining reflective.

chapter_title:
CHAPTER VI

A CAMP OF THE RESERVE
text:
“Personal feeling is misleading you,” Rhoda pursued. “Miss Royston had
a certain cleverness, I grant; but do you think I didn’t know that she
would never become what you hoped? All her spare time was given to
novel-reading. If every novelist could be strangled and thrown into the
sea we should have some chance of reforming women. The girl’s nature
was corrupted with sentimentality, like that of all but every woman who
is intelligent enough to read what is called the best fiction, but not
intelligent enough to understand its vice. Love—love—love; a
sickening sameness of vulgarity. What is more vulgar than the ideal of
novelists? They won’t represent the actual world; it would be too dull
for their readers. In real life, how many men and women  fall in love ?
Not one in every ten thousand, I am convinced. Not one married pair in
ten thousand have felt for each other as two or three couples do in
every novel. There is the sexual instinct, of course, but that is quite
a different thing; the novelists daren’t talk about that. The paltry
creatures daren’t tell the one truth that would be profitable. The
result is that women imagine themselves noble and glorious when they
are most near the animals. This Miss Royston—when she rushed off to
perdition, ten to one she had in mind some idiot heroine of a book. Oh,
I tell you that you are losing sight of your first duty. There are
people enough to act the good Samaritan;  you  have quite another task
in life. It is your work to train and encourage girls in a path as far
as possible from that of the husband-hunter. Let them marry later, if
they must; but at all events you will have cleared their views on the
subject of marriage, and put them in a position to judge the man who
offers himself. You will have taught them that marriage is an alliance
of intellects—not a means of support, or something more ignoble still.
But to do this with effect you must show yourself relentless to female
imbecility. If a girl gets to know that you have received back such a
person as Miss Royston she will be corrupted by your spirit of
charity—corrupted, at all events, for our purposes. The endeavour to
give women a new soul is so difficult that we can’t be cumbered by
side-tasks, such as fishing foolish people out of the mud they have
walked into. Charity for human weakness is all very well in its place,
but it is precisely one of the virtues that you must  not  teach. You
have to set an example of the sterner qualities—to discourage anything
that resembles sentimentalism. And think if you illustrate in your own
behaviour a sympathy for the very vice of character we are trying our
hardest to extirpate!”

enrichment.interest_rationale: Rhoda's passionate harangue: she attacks Bella's sentimentality, blames novels for corrupting women, defends a strict ideal, frames the work as transformation of female nature itself; reveals her ideological intensity, anti-romantic fervor, and contempt for 'female imbecility'—the chapter's most extended and vivid expression of Rhoda's radical asceticism.
enrichment.best_quote: If every novelist could be strangled and thrown into the sea we should have some chance of reforming women.
enrichment.summary: Rhoda argues that Bella was corrupted by sentimental novels that misrepresent love; she attacks sentimentality and the romantic ideal as enemies of female progress; warns that readmitting Bella would teach charity instead of the stern virtues needed for true emancipation.

chapter_title:
CHAPTER VI

A CAMP OF THE RESERVE
text:
“This is a terrible harangue,” said Miss Barfoot, when the passionate
voice had been silent for a few ticks of the clock. “I quite enter into
your point of view, but I think you go beyond practical zeal. However,
I will help the girl in some other way, if possible.”

enrichment.interest_rationale: Barfoot's response: the harangue is 'terrible' but she cannot dismiss Rhoda's seriousness; she concedes on the practical point but resolves to help Bella otherwise.
enrichment.summary: Barfoot acknowledges Rhoda's sincerity and shares some views, but believes Rhoda goes too far; she concedes not to bring Bella back but promises to help her otherwise.

chapter_title:
CHAPTER VI

A CAMP OF THE RESERVE
text: “I have offended you.”

enrichment.interest_rationale: Rhoda's brief inquiry whether she has caused offence; minimal content.
enrichment.summary: Rhoda asks whether she has offended Barfoot.

chapter_title:
CHAPTER VI

A CAMP OF THE RESERVE
text: “Impossible to take offence at such obvious sincerity.”

enrichment.interest_rationale: Barfoot's gentle reply: the sincerity of Rhoda's position prevents offence; shows Barfoot's generosity and acceptance of ideological difference.
enrichment.summary: Barfoot assures Rhoda that her obvious sincerity makes offence impossible.

chapter_title:
CHAPTER VI

A CAMP OF THE RESERVE
text: “But surely you grant the force of what I say?”

enrichment.interest_rationale: Rhoda's question whether Barfoot acknowledges the force of Rhoda's argument; seeks validation but minimal substantive content.
enrichment.summary: Rhoda asks whether Barfoot at least grants the force of her argument.

chapter_title:
CHAPTER VI

A CAMP OF THE RESERVE
text:
“We differ a good deal, Rhoda, on certain points which as a rule would
never come up to interfere with our working in harmony. You have come
to dislike the very thought of marriage—and everything of that kind. I
think it’s a danger you ought to have avoided. True, we wish to prevent
girls from marrying just for the sake of being supported, and from
degrading themselves as poor Bella Royston has done; but surely between
ourselves we can admit that the vast majority of women would lead a
wasted life if they did not marry.”

enrichment.interest_rationale: Barfoot's measured rebuttal: she and Rhoda differ fundamentally on marriage's necessity; Barfoot defends human nature against institutional critique; suggests Rhoda's rejection of marriage is both intellectually extreme and personally dangerous.
enrichment.best_quote: You have come to dislike the very thought of marriage—and everything of that kind. I think it's a danger you ought to have avoided.
enrichment.summary: Barfoot argues that Rhoda has gone too far in rejecting marriage and all it entails; she asserts that most women would lead wasted lives if they did not marry and that Rhoda's position is dangerous.

chapter_title:
CHAPTER VI

A CAMP OF THE RESERVE
text:
“I maintain that the vast majority of women lead a vain and miserable
life because they  do  marry.”

enrichment.interest_rationale: Rhoda's blunt rebuttal: marriage itself, not circumstance, makes women's lives vain and miserable; frames the institution as fundamentally oppressive. Stark articulation of her anti-marriage ideology.
enrichment.best_quote: I maintain that the vast majority of women lead a vain and miserable life because they do marry.
enrichment.summary: Rhoda insists that marriage itself, not bad luck or poor choice, causes women's misery.

A CAMP OF THE RESERVE

“Winifred has much good sense,” admitted the other. “I think she is in
as little danger as any girl we know. But it wouldn’t startle me if she
made the most lamentable mistake. Certainly I don’t fear it. The girls
of our class are not like the uneducated, who, for one reason or
another, will marry almost any man rather than remain single. They have
at all events personal delicacy. But what I insist upon is, that
Winifred would rather marry than not. And we must carefully bear that
fact in mind. A strained ideal is as bad, practically, as no ideal at
all. Only the most exceptional girl will believe it her duty to remain
single as an example and support to what we call the odd women; yet
 that  is the most human way of urging what you desire. By taking up
the proud position that a woman must be altogether independent of
sexual things, you damage your cause. Let us be glad if we put a few of
them in the way of living single with no more discontent than an
unmarried man experiences.”

enrichment.interest_rationale: Barfoot's long, nuanced final statement: she defends Winifred's good sense while insisting she would *prefer* marriage, acknowledges the danger of strained ideals, and defines the best approach as one that prepares girls to judge marriage rationally while accepting its probability—humanistic feminism versus ascetic purism.
enrichment.best_quote: By taking up the proud position that a woman must be altogether independent of sexual things, you damage your cause. Let us be glad if we put a few of them in the way of living single with no more discontent than an unmarried man experiences.
enrichment.summary: Barfoot defends Winifred's capacity for judgment while asserting that most women would prefer marriage; she argues that a strained ascetic ideal damages feminism and that the true goal is contentment for the unmarried, not enforced celibacy.

chapter_title:

A CAMP OF THE RESERVE

“Surely that’s an unfortunate comparison,” said Rhoda coldly. “What man
lives in celibacy? Consider that unmentionable fact, and then say
whether I am wrong in refusing to forgive Miss Royston. Women’s battle
is not only against themselves. The necessity of the case demands what
you call a strained ideal. I am seriously convinced that before the
female sex can be raised from its low level there will have to be a
widespread revolt against sexual instinct. Christianity couldn’t spread
over the world without help of the ascetic ideal, and this great
movement for woman’s emancipation must also have its ascetics.”

enrichment.interest_rationale: Rhoda's final major statement: she challenges Barfoot's comparison, pointing out that men's celibacy is rare due to sexual freedom; she frames women's emancipation as requiring ascetic resistance to sexual instinct, analogous to Christianity's ascetic ideal. The ideological climax of the debate.
enrichment.best_quote: The necessity of the case demands what you call a strained ideal. I am seriously convinced that before the female sex can be raised from its low level there will have to be a widespread revolt against sexual instinct.
enrichment.summary: Rhoda rejects Barfoot's comparison, pointing out that men escape celibacy through sexual access; she insists that female emancipation requires ascetic resistance to sexual instinct, framing it as necessary as Christianity's ascetic ideal.

enrichment.interest_rationale: Barfoot's final concession: she cannot declare Rhoda wrong but insists that such ascetic doctrine should not be preached to pupils; pragmatic retreat on principle.
enrichment.summary: Barfoot grants that Rhoda may be right philosophically but insists such ascetic ideals should not be taught to their pupils.

chapter_title:

A CAMP OF THE RESERVE
text:
“My dear,” said the elder woman gravely, “believe me that the less we
talk or think about such things the better for the peace of us all. The
odious fault of working-class girls, in town and country alike, is that
they are absorbed in preoccupation with their animal nature. We, thanks
to our education and the tone of our society, manage to keep that in
the background. Don’t interfere with this satisfactory state of things.
Be content to show our girls that it is their duty to lead a life of
effort—to earn their bread and to cultivate their minds. Simply ignore
marriage—that’s the wisest. Behave as if the thing didn’t exist. You
will do positive harm by taking the other course—the aggressive
course.”

enrichment.interest_rationale: Barfoot's long, final statement: she urges silence on sexual matters, observes that educated women are fortunately distanced from 'animal nature' through culture and education, and warns against Rhoda's aggressive course. Reveals tension between female emancipation and domestication.
enrichment.best_quote: Simply ignore marriage—that's the wisest. Behave as if the thing didn't exist.
enrichment.summary: Barfoot advises silence on marriage and sexual matters, noting that educated women are fortuitously protected from base preoccupation with the animal; she warns against Rhoda's aggressive strategy.

hardest to do no more than smile appreciation. My laugh compelled Mrs.
Poppleton to stare at me—oh, her eyes! Thereupon, her husband began
his dread performance. The patience, the heroic patience, of that dear,
good fellow! I have known him explain, and re-explain, for a quarter of
an hour, and invariably without success. It might be a mere pun; Mrs.
Poppleton no more understood the nature of a pun than of the binomial
theorem. But worse was when the jest involved some allusion. When I
heard Poppleton begin to elucidate, to expound, the perspiration
already on his forehead, I looked at him with imploring anguish. Why

disregard his wife’s request. Shall I ever forget her. “Oh—yes—I
see”?—when obviously she saw nothing but the wall at which she sat
staring.”

enrichment.interest_rationale: A masterpiece of comic narration: Everard's extended anecdote of Poppleton's martyrdom to his wife's stupidity is brilliant, savage, and enormously quotable. The passage exposes Everard's contempt for female incompetence while implicitly indicting marriage itself. It is both darkly comic and thematically central to the novel's exploration of gender, marriage, and male resentment.

enrichment.summary: Everard elaborates the torture of Poppleton's marriage through extended comic detail: his friend's endless, futile attempts to explain jokes to his wife's blank incomprehension, culminating in the image of her staring unseeing at the wall.

found that he had abandoned all his possessions to Mrs. Orchard, and
just kept himself alive on casual work for the magazines, wandering
about the shores of the Mediterranean like an uneasy spirit. He showed
me the thing he had last written, and I see it is published in this
month’s  Macmillan . Do read it. An exquisite description of a night in

enrichment.interest_rationale: Mary's direct challenge to Everard; functional dialogue advancing argument.

“Let me give an account of a day I spent with him at Tintern, not long
before I left England. He and his wife were having a holiday there, and
I called on them. We went to walk about the Abbey. Now, for some two
hours—I will be strictly truthful—whilst we were in the midst of that
lovely scenery, Mrs. Orchard discoursed unceasingly of one subject—the
difficulty she had with her domestic servants. Ten or twelve of these
handmaidens were marshalled before our imagination; their names, their
ages, their antecedents, the wages they received, were carefully
specified. We listened to a  catalogue raisonne  of the plates, cups,
and other utensils that they had broken. We heard of the enormities
which in each case led to their dismissal. Orchard tried repeatedly to
change the subject, but only with the effect of irritating his wife.
What could he or I do but patiently give ear? Our walk was ruined, but
there was no help for it. Now, be good enough to extend this kind of
thing over a number of years. Picture Orchard sitting down in his home
to literary work, and liable at any moment to an invasion from Mrs.

charged for a joint they have not consumed—or something of that kind.

firmly believed him.”

text:
“It amounted to that. From quite a child, Everard was at odds with his
father. A strange thing, for in so many respects they resembled each
other very closely. Physically, Everard is his father walking the earth
again. In character, too, I think they must be very much alike. They
couldn’t talk about the simplest thing without disagreeing. My uncle
had risen from the ranks but he disliked to be reminded of it. He
disliked the commerce by which he made his fortune. His desire was to
win social position; if baronetcies could be purchased in our time, he
would have given a huge sum to acquire one. But he never distinguished
himself, and one of the reasons was, no doubt, that he married too
soon. I have heard him speak bitterly, and very indiscreetly, of early
marriages; his wife was dead then, but every one knew what he meant.
Rhoda, when one thinks how often a woman is a clog upon a man’s
ambition, no wonder they regard us as they do.”

enrichment.interest_rationale: Extended exposition of Everard's family history, his father's character, his father's marriage regret, and the observation that 'a woman is often a clog upon a man's ambition.' This passage reveals the ideological fault lines—Mary sympathizes with the father's resentment and makes a statement that endorses the notion that women hinder male achievement. It is thematically dense and misogynistic.
enrichment.best_quote: Rhoda, when one thinks how often a woman is a clog upon a man's ambition, no wonder they regard us as they do.
enrichment.summary: Mary explains Everard's early conflict with his father, his father's rise from ranks and desire for social position, his regret over early marriage, and notes that women often impede male ambition.

text:
“Of course, women are always retarding one thing or another. But men
are intensely stupid not to have remedied that long ago.”

enrichment.interest_rationale: Rhoda's agreement that women retard things but blame for male stupidity in not remedying the situation; brief but pointed.
enrichment.best_quote: Of course, women are always retarding one thing or another. But men are intensely stupid not to have remedied that long ago.
enrichment.summary: Rhoda concedes that women retard male progress but asserts men are stupid for not having resolved the problem.

text:
“He determined that his boys should be gentlemen. Tom, the elder,
followed his wishes exactly; he was remarkably clever, but idleness
spoilt him, and now he has made that ridiculous marriage—the end of
poor Tom. Everard went to Eton, and the school had a remarkable effect
upon him; it made him a furious Radical. Instead of imitating the young
aristocrats he hated and scorned them. There must have been great force
of originality in the boy. Of course I don’t know whether any Etonians
of his time preached Radicalism, but it seems unlikely. I think it was
sheer vigour of character, and the strange desire to oppose his father
in everything. From Eton he was of course to pass to Oxford, but at
that stage came practical rebellion. No, said the boy; he wouldn’t go
to a university, to fill his head with useless learning; he had made up
his mind to be an engineer. This was an astonishment to every one;
engineering didn’t seem at all the thing for him; he had very little
ability in mathematics, and his bent had always been to liberal
studies. But nothing could shake his idea. He had got it into his head
that only some such work as engineering—something of a practical kind,
that called for strength and craftsmanship—was worthy of a man with
his opinions. He would rank with the classes that keep the world going
with their sturdy toil: that was how he spoke. And, after a great
fight, he had his way. He left Eton to study civil engineering.”

enrichment.interest_rationale: Extended, fascinating narrative of Everard's youth: his rebellion at Eton, his Radicalism, his deliberate rejection of Oxford for engineering despite unsuitability, his stubborn commitment to work he loathed for years out of refusal to admit error. This passage is central to understanding Everard's character—his force of will, his need to oppose his father, his capacity for self-torture. It is brilliantly narrated and thematically crucial to the novel.
enrichment.best_quote: He would rank with the classes that keep the world going with their sturdy toil: that was how he spoke. And, after a great fight, he had his way. He left Eton to study civil engineering.
enrichment.summary: Mary recounts Everard's Radical rejection of Oxford in favor of engineering, his lack of mathematical ability, and his stubborn commitment to a profession unsuited to him out of sheer will to oppose his father.

text: Rhoda was listening with an amused smile.

enrichment.interest_rationale: Rhoda's amused smile at the account; brief reaction.
enrichment.summary: Rhoda listens with an amused smile.

text:
“Then,” pursued her friend, “came another display of firmness or
obstinacy, whichever you like to call it. He soon found out that he had
made a complete mistake. The studies didn’t suit him at all, as others
had foreseen. But he would have worked himself to death rather than
confess his error; none of us knew how he was feeling till long after.
Engineering he had chosen, and an engineer he would be, cost him what
effort it might. His father shouldn’t triumph over him. And from the
age of eighteen till nearly thirty he stuck to a profession which I am
sure he loathed. By force of resolve he even got on to it, and reached
a good position with the firm he worked for. Of course his father
wouldn’t assist him with money after he came of age; he had to make his
way just like any young man who has no influence.”

enrichment.interest_rationale: Continuation of Everard's biography: he discovered engineering unsuited to him but refused to confess error, maintaining commitment through sheer will until nearly thirty. He reached good position despite his father's refusal to help. The passage reveals his stubborn honor and capacity for self-sacrifice to pride.
enrichment.best_quote: He would have worked himself to death rather than confess his error; none of us knew how he was feeling till long after. Engineering he had chosen, and an engineer he would be, cost him what effort it might. His father shouldn't triumph over him.
enrichment.summary: Mary describes Everard's silent suffering in engineering work, his refusal to admit mistake, and his achievement of a good position despite his father's abandonment.

text: “All this puts him in quite another light,” remarked Rhoda.

enrichment.interest_rationale: Rhoda's brief observation that the account places Everard in a better light; functional response.
enrichment.summary: Rhoda notes that this history casts Everard in a more favorable light.

text:
“Yes, it would be all very well, if there were no vices to add to the
picture. I never experienced such a revulsion of feeling as the day
when I learnt shameful things about Everard. You know, I always
regarded him as a boy, and very much as if he had been my younger
brother; then came the shock—a shock that had a great part in shaping
my life thenceforward. Since, I have thought of him as I have spoken of
him to you—as an illustration of evils we have to combat. A man of the
world would tell you that I grossly magnified trifles; it is very
likely that Everard was on a higher moral level than most men. But I
shall never forgive him for destroying my faith in his honour and
nobility of feeling.”

enrichment.interest_rationale: Mary's revelation of moral failure that profoundly shocked her: Everard was 'vicious and cowardly,' which shattered her faith in his honor. She frames this as central to her lifelong judgment of him. The vagueness is strategic—the reader never learns the exact nature of his transgression, but it was serious enough to reshape Mary's life.
enrichment.best_quote: I never experienced such a revulsion of feeling as the day when I learnt shameful things about Everard... Since, I have thought of him as I have spoken of him to you—as an illustration of evils we have to combat.
enrichment.summary: Mary reveals she learned shameful things about Everard that shattered her belief in his honor and shaped her feminist convictions.

text: Rhoda had a puzzled look.

enrichment.interest_rationale: Rhoda's puzzled response; minimal dialogue.
enrichment.summary: Rhoda looks puzzled.

enrichment.interest_rationale: Rhoda's probe asking whether Mary has been unintentionally misleading her; implies Rhoda expected worse.

text:
“If society were really decent, he would have been. It’s strange how
completely his Radicalism has disappeared. I believe he never had a
genuine sympathy with the labouring classes. And what’s more, I fancy
he had a great deal of his father’s desire for command and social
distinction. If he had seen his way to become a great engineer, a
director of vast enterprises, he wouldn’t have abandoned his work. An
incredible stubbornness has possibly spoilt his whole life. In a
congenial pursuit he might by this time have attained to something
noteworthy. It’s too late now, I fear.”

enrichment.interest_rationale: Mary's assessment of Everard's current state: his Radicalism was never genuine, and he shared his father's desire for command and distinction. Had he succeeded as an engineer, he would have continued. His stubbornness has spoiled his potential. This passage synthesizes Mary's view of Everard as trapped by his own character.
enrichment.best_quote: An incredible stubbornness has possibly spoilt his whole life.
enrichment.summary: Mary suggests Everard's Radicalism was shallow, that he shares his father's ambition for power, and that his stubbornness has wasted his life's potential.

“He won’t admit any ambition. He has no society. His friends are nearly

text:
“After all, what ambition should he have?” said Rhoda, with a laugh.
“There’s one advantage in being a woman. A woman with brains and will
may hope to distinguish herself in the greatest movement of our
time—that of emancipating her sex. But what can a man do, unless he
has genius?”

enrichment.interest_rationale: Rhoda's spirited defense of ambitionlessness: a woman can achieve distinction through women's emancipation, the great cause of their time, but men without genius have no worthy sphere. This passage articulates the novel's central theme—that women have a noble cause while men are left with only materialism or idle pleasure. Highly quotable and thematically essential.
enrichment.best_quote: There's one advantage in being a woman. A woman with brains and will may hope to distinguish herself in the greatest movement of our time—that of emancipating her sex. But what can a man do, unless he has genius?
enrichment.summary: Rhoda argues that women have the great cause of emancipation available to them, but men without genius have no worthy sphere.

“There’s the emancipation of the working classes. That is the great

enrichment.best_quote: There's the emancipation of the working classes. That is the great sphere for men; and Everard cares no more for the working classes than I do.
enrichment.summary: Mary suggests the working-class movement as man's equivalent cause but notes Everard has no interest in it.

enrichment.summary: Mary's expression brightens with a glad realization.

text:
“You are right. It’s better to be a woman, in our day. With us is all
the joy of advance, the glory of conquering. Men have only material
progress to think about. But we—we are winning souls, propagating a
new religion, purifying the earth!”

enrichment.interest_rationale: Mary's rhapsodic affirmation of women's superiority: women are winning souls, propagating a new religion, purifying the earth, while men are left with mere material progress. enrichment.best_quote: But we—we are winning souls, propagating a new religion, purifying the earth!
enrichment.summary: Mary exults that women have the joy of advance and glory of conquest, while men have only material progress; women are purifying the earth through emancipation.

enrichment.summary: Rhoda nods three times in agreement.

text:
“My cousin is a fine specimen of a man, after all, in body and mind.
But what a poor, ineffectual creature compared with  you , Rhoda! I
don’t flatter you, dear. I tell you bluntly of your faults and
extravagances. But I am proud of your magnificent independence, proud
of your pride, dear, and of your stainless heart. Thank Heaven we are
women!”

enrichment.interest_rationale: Mary's climactic affirmation of Rhoda's magnificent independence, pride, and stainless heart, ending with gratitude that they are women. This passage celebrates Rhoda as ideal and concludes the chapter on a note of female solidarity and mutual admiration. It is emotionally powerful and thematically culminating.
enrichment.best_quote: Thank Heaven we are women!
enrichment.summary: Mary praises Rhoda's magnificent independence, pride, and stainless heart, declaring gratitude for their womanhood.

text:
It was rare indeed for Miss Barfoot to be moved to rhapsody. Again
Rhoda nodded, and then they laughed together, with joyous confidence in
themselves and in their cause.

enrichment.interest_rationale: Final paragraph: Mary's rhapsody is rare; the women laugh together with joyous confidence in themselves and their cause. The chapter ends on celebratory note of female solidarity, providing counterweight to Everard's seductive charm and setting up the tension to come.
enrichment.summary: The friends laugh together with joyous confidence in themselves and their feminist cause, a rare moment of rhapsody from Mary.

text:
Seated in the reading-room of a club to which he had newly procured
admission, Everard Barfoot was glancing over the advertisement columns
of a literary paper. His eye fell on an announcement that had a
personal interest to him, and at once he went to the writing-table to
pen a letter.

enrichment.interest_rationale: Routine expository setup establishing Everard's location and action.
enrichment.summary: Everard Barfoot sits in a club reading-room and notices an advertisement that prompts him to write a letter.

text:
“DEAR MICKLETHWAITE,—I am back in England, and ought before this to
have written to you. I see you have just published a book with an
alarming title, “A Treatise on Trilinear Co-ordinates.” My hearty
congratulations on the completion of such a labour; were you not the
most disinterested of mortals, I would add a hope that it may somehow
benefit you financially. I presume there  are  people who purchase such
works. But of course the main point with you is to have delivered your
soul on Trilinear Co-ordinates. Shall I run down to Sheffield to see
you, or is there any chance of the holidays bringing you this way? I
have found a cheap flat, poorly furnished, in Bayswater; the man who
let it to me happens to be an engineer, and is absent on Italian
railway work for a year or so. My stay in London won’t, I think, be for
longer than six months, but we must see each other and talk over old
times,” etc.

enrichment.interest_rationale: The letter reveals Everard's wit and casual tone, establishing his personality and recent return to London, with hints of his housing situation and brief intended stay.
enrichment.best_quote: were you not the most disinterested of mortals, I would add a hope that it may somehow benefit you financially
enrichment.summary: Everard writes to Thomas Micklethwaite congratulating him on publishing a mathematical treatise and proposing to meet, mentioning his temporary London lodgings.

text:
This he addressed to a school at Sheffield. The answer, directed to the
club, reached him in three days.

enrichment.interest_rationale: Simple narrative transition noting the letter's dispatch and receipt.
enrichment.summary: Everard's letter reaches Micklethwaite at his club within three days.

text:
“My DEAR BARFOOT,—I also am in London; your letter has been forwarded
from the school, which I quitted last Easter. Disinterested or not, I
am happy to tell you that I have got a vastly better appointment. Let
me know when and where to meet you; or if you like, come to these
lodgings of mine. I don’t enter upon duties till end of October, and am
at present revelling in mathematical freedom. There’s a great deal to
tell.—Sincerely yours,

enrichment.interest_rationale: Micklethwaite's reply is routine exposition revealing his improved circumstances and London presence, advancing the narrative minimally.
enrichment.summary: Micklethwaite writes back from London confirming he has left Sheffield for a better position and suggesting they meet.

text: THOMAS MICKLETHWAITE.”

text:
Having no occupation for his morning, Barfoot went at once to the
obscure little street by Primrose Hill where his friend was lodging. He
reached the house about noon, and, as he had anticipated, found the
mathematician deep in study. Micklethwaite was a man of forty, bent in
the shoulders, sallow, but not otherwise of unhealthy appearance; he
had a merry countenance, a great deal of lank, disorderly hair, and a
beard that reached to the middle of his waistcoat. Everard’s
acquaintance with him dated from ten years ago, when Micklethwaite had
acted as his private tutor in mathematics.

enrichment.interest_rationale: Physical description of Micklethwaite and backstory of his friendship with Everard establish character and history efficiently.
enrichment.summary: Everard visits Micklethwaite in his Primrose Hill lodgings and finds him studying; the narrator describes Micklethwaite's appearance and notes they met ten years ago as tutor and student.

text: The room was a musty little back-parlour on the ground floor.

enrichment.interest_rationale: Minimal description of Micklethwaite's shabby living quarters; purely expository.
enrichment.summary: Micklethwaite's room is described as a small, musty back-parlour on the ground floor.

text:
“Quiet, perfectly quiet,” declared its occupant, “and that’s all I care
for. Two other lodgers in the house; but they go to business every
morning at half-past eight, and are in bed by ten at night. Besides,
it’s only temporary. I have great things in view—portentous changes!
I’ll tell you all about it presently.”

enrichment.interest_rationale: Micklethwaite's satisfaction with quiet and cryptic allusion to 'portentous changes' create intrigue and hint at the central secret of the conversation to come.
enrichment.best_quote: I have great things in view—portentous changes!
enrichment.summary: Micklethwaite describes his contentment with his quiet lodgings and hints at significant changes coming soon.

text:
He insisted, first of all, on hearing a full account of Barfoot’s
history since they both met. They had corresponded about twice a year,
but Everard was not fond of letter-writing, and on each occasion gave
only the briefest account of himself. In listening, Micklethwaite
assumed extraordinary positions, the result, presumably, of a need of
physical exercise after hours spent over his work. Now he stretched
himself at full length on the edge of his chair, his arms extended
above him; now he drew up his legs, fixed his feet on the chair, and
locked his hands round his knees; thus perched, he swayed his body
backwards and forwards, till it seemed likely that he would pitch head
foremost on to the floor. Barfoot knew these eccentricities of old, and
paid no attention to them.

enrichment.interest_rationale: Physical comedy of Micklethwaite's eccentric postures while listening; characterization through mannerism.
enrichment.summary: As Everard speaks, Micklethwaite adopts contorted positions in his chair, a habit Everard is accustomed to.

text:

enrichment.interest_rationale: Everard's response reveals he would be capable of manipulation if his intended target were wealthy, indicating his morality is conditional on economics.
enrichment.best_quote: If she were rich, I think I could do it without scruple.
enrichment.summary: Everard suggests he would have no qualms about seducing Rhoda Nunn if she were wealthy.

text:
“You seem to be taking it for granted,” said the mathematician,
smiling, “that this lady would—would respond to your love-making.”

enrichment.interest_rationale: Micklethwaite's amused observation that Everard assumes Rhoda would reciprocate reveals his confidence in his attractiveness, which is important to understanding his character.
enrichment.best_quote: You seem to be taking it for granted that this lady would—would respond to your love-making.
enrichment.summary: Micklethwaite smilingly suggests Everard is confident that Rhoda would respond to his courtship.

text:
“I confess to you that women have spoilt me. And I am rather resentful
when any one cries out against me for lack of respect to womanhood. I
have been the victim of this groundless veneration for females. Now you
shall hear the story; and bear in mind that you are the only person to
whom I have ever told it. I never tried to defend myself when I was
vilified on all hands. Probably the attempt would have been useless;
and then it would certainly have increased the odium in which I stood.
I think I’ll tell cousin Mary the truth some day; it would be good for
her.”

enrichment.interest_rationale: Everard's extended reflection on his experience with women, his lack of respect for them, his victimization by 'veneration,' and his resolve to finally tell the truth is foundational to his character and the novel's psychology.
enrichment.best_quote: I confess to you that women have spoilt me. And I am rather resentful when any one cries out against me for lack of respect to womanhood. I have been the victim of this groundless veneration for females.
enrichment.summary: Everard confesses that women have spoiled him through excessive admiration; he resents being criticized for disrespecting them while claiming victimhood to their veneration; he mentions telling his cousin the truth someday.

text: The listener looked uneasy, but curious.

enrichment.interest_rationale: The narrator notes Micklethwaite's unsettled curiosity, setting up the long narrative that follows.
enrichment.summary: Micklethwaite looks uneasy but curious as Everard prepares to tell his story.

text:
“Well now, I was staying in the summer with some friends of ours at a
little place called Upchurch, on a branch line from Oxford. The people
were well-to-do—Goodall their name—and went in for philanthropy. Mrs.
Goodall always had a lot of Upchurch girls about her, educated and not;
her idea was to civilize one class by means of the other, and to give a
new spirit to both. My cousin Mary was staying at the house whilst I
was there. She had more reasonable views than Mrs. Goodall, but took a
great interest in what was going on.

enrichment.interest_rationale: Everard's background exposition on the Goodall family's social experiment and Mary's involvement establishes context for the scandal, showing wealth-based philanthropy.
enrichment.summary: Everard describes staying with the philanthropic Goodall family at Upchurch during a summer, where they attempted to 'civilize' local girls of different classes.

text:
“Now one of the girls in process of spiritualization was called Amy
Drake. In the ordinary course of things I shouldn’t have met her, but
she served in a shop where I went two or three times to get a
newspaper; we talked a little—with absolute propriety on my part, I
assure you—and she knew that I was a friend of the Goodalls. The girl
had no parents, and she was on the point of going to London to live
with a married sister.

enrichment.interest_rationale: Everard's introduction of Amy Drake and their initial interaction establishes her as the catalyst for scandal; his claim of propriety contrasts with later revelation.
enrichment.summary: Everard describes meeting Amy Drake, an orphaned shop girl, who knew of his connection to the Goodalls and was about to leave for London.

text:
“It happened that by the very train which took me back to London, when
my visit was over, this girl also travelled, and alone. I saw her at
Upchurch Station, but we didn’t speak, and I got into a smoking
carriage. We had to change at Oxford, and there, as I walked about the
platform, Amy put herself in my way, so that I was obliged to begin
talking with her. This behaviour rather surprised me. I wondered what
Mrs. Goodall would think of it. But perhaps it was a sign of innocent
freedom in the intercourse of men and women. At all events, Amy managed
to get me into the same carriage with herself, and on the way to London
we were alone. You foresee the end of it. At Paddington Station the
girl and I went off together, and she didn’t get to her sister’s till
the evening.

enrichment.interest_rationale: Everard's account of Amy's forwardness on the train journey and their intimate encounter at Paddington is crucial plot revelation; his tone suggests seduction or consent remains ambiguous to him.
enrichment.best_quote: You foresee the end of it. At Paddington Station the girl and I went off together, and she didn't get to her sister's till the evening.
enrichment.summary: Everard describes how Amy deliberately positioned herself to travel with him alone to London and they became intimate at Paddington, departing from her planned arrival.

text:
“Of course I take it for granted that you believe my account of the
matter. Miss Drake was by no means the spiritual young person that Mrs.
Goodall thought her, or hoped to make her; plainly, she was a reprobate
of experience. This, you will say, doesn’t alter the fact that I also
behaved like a reprobate. No; from the moralist’s point of view I was
to blame. But I had no moral pretentions, and it was too much to expect
that I should rebuke the young woman and preach her a sermon. You admit
that, I dare say?”

enrichment.interest_rationale: Everard's admission that Amy was experienced and his justification that he took no moral responsibility is central to understanding his character and moral framework.
enrichment.best_quote: Of course I take it for granted that you believe my account of the matter. Miss Drake was by no means the spiritual young person that Mrs. Goodall thought her, or hoped to make her; plainly, she was a reprobate of experience.
enrichment.summary: Everard insists Amy was experienced, not innocent, and thus he bore no responsibility for seducing her as she was already a 'reprobate.'

text: The mathematician, frowning uncomfortably, gave a nod of assent.

enrichment.interest_rationale: Micklethwaite's simple nod of uncomfortable assent.
enrichment.summary: Micklethwaite nods in uncomfortable agreement.

text:
“Amy was not only a reprobate, but a rascal. She betrayed me to the
people at Upchurch, and, I am quite sure, meant from the first to do
so. Imagine the outcry. I had committed a monstrous crime—had led
astray an innocent maiden, had outraged hospitality—and so on. In
Amy’s case there were awkward results. Of course I must marry the girl
forthwith. But of course I was determined to do no such thing. For the
reasons I have explained, I let the storm break upon me. I had been a
fool, to be sure, and couldn’t help myself. No one would have believed
my plea—no one would have allowed that the truth was an excuse. I was
abused on all hands. And when, shortly after, my father made his will
and died, doubtless he cut me off with my small annuity on this very
account. My cousin Mary got a good deal of the money that would
otherwise have been mine. The old man had been on rather better terms
with me just before that; in a will that he destroyed I believe he had
treated me handsomely.”

enrichment.interest_rationale: Everard's account of Amy's betrayal, her accusation that he seduced her innocently, the social outcry, and his father's disinheritance reveal the scandal's consequences and his family's judgment of his character.
enrichment.best_quote: Amy was not only a reprobate, but a rascal. She betrayed me to the people at Upchurch, and, I am quite sure, meant from the first to do so. Imagine the outcry. I had committed a monstrous crime—had led astray an innocent maiden, had outraged hospitality—and so on.
enrichment.summary: Amy betrayed Everard by falsely claiming innocence and accusing him of seduction; public outcry ensued; he refused to marry her; his father disinherited him partly for this cause.

text:
“Well, well,” said Micklethwaite, “every one knows there are detestable
women to be found. But you oughtn’t to let this affect your view of
women in general. What became of the girl?”

enrichment.interest_rationale: Micklethwaite's moral counsel that Everard should not let this affair affect his view of women, while acknowledging detestable women exist.
enrichment.summary: Micklethwaite acknowledges detestable women exist but argues Everard should not generalize from his experience.

text:
“I made her a small allowance for a year and a half. Then her child
died, and the allowance ceased. I know nothing more of her. Probably
she has inveigled some one into marriage.”

enrichment.interest_rationale: Everard's terse account of Amy's fate—a brief allowance, her child's death, presumed remarriage—shows his distance from consequences, treating her as a detail of his past.
enrichment.summary: Everard paid Amy an allowance for eighteen months; her child died; he ceased payments and knows nothing further of her.

text:
“Well, Barfoot,” said the other, rolling about in his chair, “my
opinion remains the same. You are in debt to some worthy woman to the
extent of half your income. Be quick and find her. It will be better
for you.”

enrichment.interest_rationale: Micklethwaite's response that Everard owes marriage to a worthy woman as recompense; moralistic but expected.
enrichment.summary: Micklethwaite suggests Everard should marry a worthy woman as compensation for his past conduct.

text:
“And do you suppose,” asked Everard, with a smile of indulgence, “that
I could marry on four hundred and fifty a year?”

enrichment.interest_rationale: Everard's bemused response that he cannot marry on £450 annually establishes his material limitations for marriage.
enrichment.summary: Everard asks if Micklethwaite supposes he could marry on £450 annually.

text: “Heavens! Why not?”

enrichment.interest_rationale: Micklethwaite's astonished question; purely dialogic.
enrichment.summary: Micklethwaite asks why not.

text:
“Quite impossible. A wife  might  be acceptable to me; but marriage
with poverty—I know myself and the world too well for that.”

enrichment.interest_rationale: Everard's final dismissal of marriage due to cost reiterates the novel's central economic constraint on marriage and women's options.
enrichment.best_quote: Grinding poverty—for married people.
enrichment.summary: Everard insists that £450 is grinding poverty for married people, and he knows himself and the world too well to attempt it.

text: “Poverty!” screamed the mathematician. “Four hundred and fifty pounds!”

enrichment.interest_rationale: Micklethwaite's incredulous protest about the amount establishes the disparity in their material expectations.
enrichment.best_quote: Grinding poverty—for married people.
enrichment.summary: Micklethwaite protests that £450 is not poverty.

text: “Grinding poverty—for married people.”

enrichment.interest_rationale: Everard's reiteration emphasizes the gulf between Micklethwaite's modest expectations and Everard's higher standard of living.
enrichment.summary: Everard reiterates it is poverty for married life.

text:
Micklethwaite burst into indignant eloquence, and Everard sat listening
with the restrained smile on his lips.

enrichment.interest_rationale: Micklethwaite's impassioned counter-argument and Everard's restrained smile bring the chapter toward closure with their ideological opposition unresolved.
enrichment.summary: Micklethwaite launches into passionate argument while Everard listens with a restrained smile.
